messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol is a 61-year-old Guatemalan American woman who has been married for thirty-four years and has worked as a city bus driver for the past eighteen. She presented for psychological evaluation approximately four months after witnessing a fatal pedestrian accident that occurred directly in front of her route on a busy urban corridor. On a Tuesday morning in early spring, Marisol was stopped at a red light when she watched a sedan run the intersection at speed and strike a woman crossing with a stroller. The impact was immediate and catastrophic. Marisol saw the woman thrown, saw the stroller overturn, saw blood spreading across the asphalt in a way she has since been unable to stop seeing. She was the first person to reach the scene. She knelt beside the woman, who was alive for several minutes, and held her hand. The infant in the stroller survived. The woman did not. Marisol has not been able to stop asking herself why she did not act faster, why she did not run into the intersection earlier, whether her hesitation — a matter of seconds — cost that woman her life. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that she had failed to protect a stranger who needed her, and that this failure was not an accident of circumstance but a revelation of her own inadequacy.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not behave like a memory. It arrived without warning and without distance. The smell of exhaust and wet pavement, the specific pitch of the impact, the warmth of the woman's hand — these returned not as recollections but as immediate sensory events. Marisol would be sitting at her kitchen table and find herself back on that asphalt, the present moment dissolving entirely. At other times there was no image at all, only a wave of grief and terror so complete that she could not speak, could not explain to her husband what was happening, could not locate its source. She had no language for the way the past kept insisting it was the present.

Returning to work became its own ordeal. Every shift placed Marisol inside the specific environment where her triggers lived most densely. A car braking hard in an adjacent lane, a pedestrian stepping off a curb at speed — these moments seized her attention with an urgency that felt like emergency rather than memory. She began performing small, private rituals before each shift: a specific sequence of words said under her breath, a particular way of touching the steering wheel, a mental checklist she believed, with quiet desperation, might prevent another catastrophe. She understood, on some level, that these rituals were not rational. She performed them anyway, because the alternative — leaving for work without them — felt like inviting disaster.

Outside of work, Marisol withdrew from physical contact with almost everyone. Her husband, a patient man who had begun sleeping in the spare room at her request, had tried to hold her hand across the dinner table and found her pulling away before she could stop herself. She did not want to be touched. She could not fully explain why, only that contact felt unbearable in a way she could not articulate. She also stopped visiting her sister, whose home contained photographs of a cousin who had died two years earlier — a loss she had grieved and largely integrated until now, when anything that reminded her of someone gone felt indistinguishable from the rawness of the spring morning. Her world had quietly contracted: fewer routes requested, fewer family dinners attended, fewer conversations completed.

What finally brought Marisol to the clinic was a conversation with her husband in which she told him, with a flatness that frightened them both, that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore. She had not made a plan. She had simply meant it, and the meaning of it scared her enough to call. She arrived at the intake appointment composed and apologetic, as though her suffering were an imposition. What she was most afraid of was that she would never stop seeing the blood, never stop believing she had failed. What she was most hoping for, though she said it quietly and without much conviction, was that she might someday be able to drive again without dread — and sit beside her husband without flinching.
